text: Trie + fail links by BFS; the trie graph.
root h s e he i h r s his e she s hers dashed: fail link

The AC automaton (AC 自动机 , Aho– Corasick) finds many patterns in one text at once. Put all patterns in a trie (第7章). Each node gets a fail link: the node for the longest proper suffix of its string that is also in the trie. It is KMP's nxt array spread over a trie.

"she" fails to "he": after reading s-h-e, the longest suffix that starts some pattern is "he". Unmarked fail links go to the root. Fail links of a node only point to shallower nodes, so a BFS by depth can fill them in order.

Build by BFS. For node u and letter c: if the child ch[u][c] exists, its fail link is ch[fail[u]][c]; if it does not exist, set ch[u][c] = ch[fail[u]][c] anyway. After that every node has a transition for every letter (a trie graph, 字典图), so matching never needs a while-loop of fail jumps.
The children of the root fail to the root. Because fail[u] is shallower than u, its row ch[fail[u]][·] is already complete when u is processed. Total O(26 · total pattern length).
Which patterns appear; how often each appears.
a aa aa
he she hers ushers

Walking the text moves u through the trie graph; at each position, the patterns ending here are u, fail[u], fail[fail[u]], … (the suffixes). Marking visited ends with −1 stops repeated walks, so each node is walked once: O(text + trie) (P3808).
In "ushers": "she" and "he" end at position 4, "hers" at 6: three different patterns appear. This early-stop trick only works because each pattern is counted at most once.

position 35 for (int i = int(order_.size()) - 1; i >= 0; i--) // deepest first: pass counts up the fail tree 36 hits[fail[order_[i]]] += hits[order_[i]]; 37 for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) cout << hits[node[i]] << "\n"; 38 return 0;

Counting every occurrence of every pattern (P5357): the fail links form a tree (the fail tree). An occurrence of pattern p ends wherever the walk stands at a node in p's fail subtree. So mark one hit per text position, then add each node's hits to its fail parent, deepest nodes first.

Reverse BFS order is a valid "children before parents" order, because a fail link always points to a shallower node. This turns O(text × depth) into O(text + trie). 单词(P3966) is the same with the patterns themselves as the text.

title: AC 自动机上的动态规划

text: Avoid or collect patterns; dangerous nodes.

DP on the automaton (AC 自动机上 DP): to count or optimise strings by which patterns they contain, use the automaton node as the DP state. f[i][u] = number of strings of length i whose walk ends at node u.
Each step tries all letters: f[i+1][ch[u][c]] += f[i][u].

Mark a node as dangerous if any pattern ends at it or at any node on its fail chain (bad[v] |= bad[fail[v]] during the BFS). Strings that avoid all patterns are the walks that never enter a dangerous node.
A B
AB
Text generator (P4052): count length-m strings that contain at least one pattern. Counting "none" is the DP above; the answer is 26m − none (complement, 第20章). With patterns A and B: 26² − 24² = 100.

Variants: is there an infinite safe string? Look for a cycle among safe nodes (P2444 病毒). Maximise points over length k: f[i][u] = best score, adding the number of patterns ending at u (P3041 Video Game, with counts accumulated along fail links).
Forgetting bad[u] |= bad[fail[u]] is the classic bug: "she" contains "he" even though the "he" end node is not on the "she" path in the trie. Do it inside the BFS, after fail[u] is known.

Deleting patterns as they appear (P3121 Censoring): keep a stack of (character, automaton node); when a pattern ends, pop its length and continue from the node now on top. The typewriter (P2414) asks "how many times does x occur in y" for many pairs: answer it on the fail tree with DFS order and a Fenwick tree.
